```{r}
#| label: diary-main-effects
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: false

# Complete-case model paths (fallback)
diary_h1_path <- "output/models/diary_model_h1_sleepquality.rds"
diary_h2_path <- "output/models/diary_model_h2_sleepquality.rds"

# H1 effects: use pooled Rubin estimates if available, else fall back to complete-case
if (!is.null(diary_h1_rubin)) {
  diary_h1_within <- get_pooled_effect(diary_h1_rubin, "ln_within_10", exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h1_between <- get_pooled_effect(diary_h1_rubin, "ln_between_10", exponentiate = FALSE)
} else {
  diary_h1_within <- get_h2_interaction(diary_h1_path, "ln_within_10", exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h1_between <- get_h2_interaction(diary_h1_path, "ln_between_10", exponentiate = FALSE)
}

# H2 effects: use pooled Rubin estimates if available, else fall back to complete-case
if (!is.null(diary_h2_rubin)) {
  diary_h2_within_chrono <- get_pooled_effect(diary_h2_rubin, "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered",
                                               exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h2_between_chrono <- get_pooled_effect(diary_h2_rubin, "chronotype_centered:ln_between_10",
                                                exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h2_chrono_main <- get_pooled_effect(diary_h2_rubin, "chronotype_centered",
                                             exponentiate = FALSE)
} else {
  diary_h2_within_chrono <- get_h2_interaction(diary_h2_path,
    "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered", exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h2_between_chrono <- get_h2_interaction(diary_h2_path,
    "chronotype_centered:ln_between_10", exponentiate = FALSE)
  diary_h2_chrono_main <- get_h2_interaction(diary_h2_path,
    "chronotype_centered", exponentiate = FALSE)
}

# Spline comparison info
diary_spline_compare_loaded <- if (file.exists("output/models/diary_spline_compare.rds")) {
  readRDS("output/models/diary_spline_compare.rds")
} else {
  NULL
}

# Render the diary df grid as "min–max" so the prose stays in sync with the
# fit chunk. Reuses the panel-side fmt_df_grid helper if available.
diary_spline_df_range <- if (!is.null(diary_spline_compare_loaded) &&
                             "df" %in% names(diary_spline_compare_loaded)) {
  if (exists("fmt_df_grid", inherits = TRUE)) {
    fmt_df_grid(diary_spline_compare_loaded$df)
  } else {
    g <- sort(unique(diary_spline_compare_loaded$df))
    if (length(g) <= 1) as.character(g[1]) else sprintf("%d–%d", min(g), max(g))
  }
} else {
  "NA"
}

# Resolve the Jones (2001) 2|ΔBIC| verdict to definite strings here so the
# prose can reference them as plain inline values (no inline conditionals).
diary_spline_jones <- list(
  twoDBIC   = NA_real_,
  favoured  = NA_character_,
  verdict   = NA_character_,
  deltaAIC  = NA_real_
)
if (!is.null(diary_spline_compare_loaded) &&
    all(c("BIC", "linear_BIC") %in% names(diary_spline_compare_loaded))) {
  .best_bic <- diary_spline_compare_loaded$BIC[1]
  .lin_bic  <- diary_spline_compare_loaded$linear_BIC[1]
  .two_dbic <- 2 * abs(.best_bic - .lin_bic)
  diary_spline_jones$twoDBIC  <- .two_dbic
  diary_spline_jones$favoured <- if (.best_bic < .lin_bic) "spline" else "linear"
  diary_spline_jones$verdict  <- if (.two_dbic < 2) {
    "not worth mentioning"
  } else if (.two_dbic < 6) {
    "positive evidence"
  } else if (.two_dbic < 10) {
    "strong evidence"
  } else {
    "very strong evidence"
  }
  diary_spline_jones$deltaAIC <- diary_spline_compare_loaded$AIC[1] -
    diary_spline_compare_loaded$linear_AIC[1]
}

if (!is.null(diary_h1_rubin)) {
  diary_h1_w  <- extract_pooled_est(diary_h1_rubin, "ln_within_10")
  diary_h1_b  <- extract_pooled_est(diary_h1_rubin, "ln_between_10")
} else {
  diary_h1_w  <- extract_clmm_est(diary_h1_path, "ln_within_10")
  diary_h1_b  <- extract_clmm_est(diary_h1_path, "ln_between_10")
}

if (!is.null(diary_h2_rubin)) {
  diary_h2_wc <- extract_pooled_est(diary_h2_rubin, "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered")
  diary_h2_bc <- extract_pooled_est(diary_h2_rubin, "chronotype_centered:ln_between_10")
  diary_h2_cm <- extract_pooled_est(diary_h2_rubin, "chronotype_centered")
} else {
  diary_h2_wc <- extract_clmm_est(diary_h2_path, "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered")
  diary_h2_bc <- extract_clmm_est(diary_h2_path, "chronotype_centered:ln_between_10")
  diary_h2_cm <- extract_clmm_est(diary_h2_path, "chronotype_centered")
}

# Marginal probability computation for diary H1 (probit CLMM, between-person)
# Use pooled estimates (Rubin's rules) when available, else single complete-case fit
diary_h1_marginal <- if (!is.null(diary_h1_rubin)) {
  tryCatch({
    pv        <- pool_vcov(diary_h1_rubin$fits)
    b_between <- pv$qbar["ln_between_10"]
    t_fair_poor <- average_re_quantity(diary_h1_rubin$fits, function(f) f$alpha["Fair|Poor"])
    sigma_u   <- average_re_quantity(diary_h1_rubin$fits, function(f) sqrt(f$ST$pid[1, 1]))
    marginal_sd <- sqrt(1 + sigma_u^2)
    pp_per_10min <- dnorm((b_between * 0 - t_fair_poor) / marginal_sd) * b_between / marginal_sd * 100
    list(pp_per_10min = pp_per_10min)
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
} else {
  tryCatch({
    m <- readRDS(diary_h1_path)
    b_between <- m$beta["ln_between_10"]
    t_fair_poor <- m$alpha["Fair|Poor"]
    sd_re <- m$ST$pid[1, 1]
    marginal_sd <- sqrt(1 + sd_re^2)
    pp_per_10min <- dnorm((b_between * 0 - t_fair_poor) / marginal_sd) * b_between / marginal_sd * 100
    list(pp_per_10min = pp_per_10min)
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
}
```

As an exploratory complement to the panel analyses, we re-used the H1a/H2a probit CLMM specification (random intercept for participant, late-night gaming scaled per 10 min/day, same covariate set) and refit it to daily diary reports of sleep quality against late-night gaming in the preceding 24 hours, rather than the 14- or 28-day averages used in the panel. Sleep quality was recorded on a 5-level ordinal scale (Very poor, Poor, Fair, Good, Very good). To separate within- from between-person variation in late-night gaming, the trimmed exposure (capped at the 99th percentile) was decomposed into a within-person component (daily deviation from the participant's own mean) and a between-person component (participant mean centred at the grand mean). The analytical diary sample comprised `r diary_n_participants` participants contributing `r format(diary_n_entries, big.mark = ",")` diary entries with valid sleep quality ratings. Region was dropped because all diary participants are US-based, and a random intercept for gender failed to converge with only three levels, so gender was excluded as well. Continuous covariates (age, BMI, SES) were rescaled within the diary subsample. Missing SES values for participants with unrecognised employment categories (n = `r diary_ses_n_missing`) were imputed via standard PMM (m = 5) using age, BMI, gender, and region as predictors. These diary analyses were not formally pre-registered.

To handle missing data in the diary outcomes and daily predictors, we applied the same hierarchical two-level `2l.pmm` approach and predictor-matrix coding as the panel imputation, with participants as clusters and diary days nested within (`miceadds`). Level-2 variables for the diary pass were age, BMI, SES, chronotype, gender, and person-mean late-night gaming; level-1 daily predictors with genuine missingness (gaming played, basic psychological needs, stress, day type, late-night gaming hours) were imputed via standard PMM within the same MICE run, and ±5-day lag and lead terms (rather than the ±1-wave terms used in the panel) provided temporal context for each outcome. We generated `r n_imputations_diary` imputed datasets with `r n_iterations_diary` iterations each — more than for the panel because of higher per-day missingness — inspected QC diagnostics and judged them acceptable, and combined diary regression estimates across imputations using Rubin's rules.

For the direct-effects model (H1), the within-person effect of late-night gaming on sleep quality was `r diary_h1_within` (probit coefficient per 10 additional minutes). On days when participants gamed more than their own average, the association with sleep quality was not statistically significant. The between-person effect was `r diary_h1_between` (probit coefficient per 10 min/day), indicating that participants who habitually engaged in more late-night gaming tended to report worse sleep quality on average; this between-person effect was statistically significant. On the probability scale, each additional 10 minutes of habitual daily late-night gaming is associated with an approximate `r fmt_pp(diary_h1_marginal)` percentage-point increase in the probability of reporting poor or very poor sleep, broadly consistent with the panel-level H1a estimate (`r fmt_pp(h1a_marginal)` pp per 10 min; @fig-diary-sleepquality, Panel A).
We compared the linear specification against natural cubic spline alternatives (df = `r diary_spline_df_range`). Among the splines, df = `r diary_spline_compare_loaded$df[1]` was preferred, but the linear model had a lower BIC by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(diary_spline_compare_loaded$BIC[1] - diary_spline_compare_loaded$linear_BIC[1]))` units (2|ΔBIC| = `r sprintf("%.1f", diary_spline_jones$twoDBIC)`) — `r diary_spline_jones$verdict` for the `r diary_spline_jones$favoured` specification under the @jones2001nagin rule of thumb. We therefore retained the linear specification, both as a parsimonious summary of the average within- and between-person associations and for direct comparability with the panel H1a/H2a estimates. Diary subsample characteristics are presented in @tbl-diary-demographics in the Appendix.

For the chronotype moderation model (H2), the interaction between within-person late-night gaming and chronotype was `r diary_h2_within_chrono`, and the interaction between between-person late-night gaming and chronotype was `r diary_h2_between_chrono`. The within-person interaction was statistically significant, indicating that the day-to-day link between late-night gaming and sleep quality was somewhat weaker for evening types. The between-person interaction was not statistically significant, suggesting that the trait-level association between habitual late-night gaming and sleep quality did not meaningfully vary across chronotypes. The main effect of chronotype was `r diary_h2_chrono_main`; a later chronotype was associated with worse sleep quality (this effect was statistically significant). These diary-based findings are exploratory and should be interpreted with caution (@fig-diary-sleepquality, Panel B).

```{r}
#| label: fig-diary-sleepquality
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability of poor sleep quality from the diary CLMM. (A) Between-person effect (H1): marginal probability of reporting Poor or Very poor sleep quality as a function of participants' average daily late-night gaming, with the within-person component held at zero. The ribbon shows 95% CIs from the between-person coefficient SE. (B) Within-person x chronotype interaction (H2): marginal probability of poor sleep quality as a function of daily within-person gaming deviation at three chronotype levels (morning = -1 SD, mean, evening = +1 SD), with the between-person component held at zero. Ribbons show 95% CIs via the delta method pooled across 60 imputations using Rubin's rules. Vertical reference lines mark the median (dotted), mean (dashed), 75th percentile (dotted), and 90th percentile (dashed) of the respective predictor distributions. Density plots (top) show predictor distributions."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 7
#| code-summary: "Diary: probability of poor sleep quality — H1 between-person & H2 within-person x chronotype"
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

diary_h1_model_available <- !is.null(diary_h1_rubin) || file.exists("output/models/diary_model_h1_sleepquality.rds")
diary_h2_model_available <- !is.null(diary_h2_rubin) || file.exists("output/models/diary_model_h2_sleepquality.rds")

if (diary_h1_model_available && diary_h2_model_available) {
  library(ordinal)
  library(patchwork)

  # ── PANEL A: H1 Between-Person Effect ──────────────────────────────────────

  ln_seq <- seq(-6, 9, by = 0.1)

  if (!is.null(diary_h1_rubin)) {
    pv_d        <- pool_vcov(diary_h1_rubin$fits)
    b_between   <- pv_d$qbar["ln_between_10"]
    se_between  <- sqrt(pv_d$vcov["ln_between_10", "ln_between_10"])
    alpha_j_d   <- average_re_quantity(diary_h1_rubin$fits, function(f) f$alpha["Fair|Poor"])
    sigma_u_d   <- average_re_quantity(diary_h1_rubin$fits, function(f) sqrt(f$ST$pid[1, 1]))
  } else {
    diary_h1_fig <- readRDS("output/models/diary_model_h1_sleepquality.rds")
    sigma_u_d   <- sqrt(diary_h1_fig$ST$pid[1, 1])
    alpha_j_d   <- diary_h1_fig$alpha["Fair|Poor"]
    b_between   <- coef(diary_h1_fig)["ln_between_10"]
    se_between  <- sqrt(vcov(diary_h1_fig)["ln_between_10", "ln_between_10"])
  }

  denom_d <- sqrt(1 + sigma_u_d^2)

  lp_d    <- b_between * ln_seq
  lp_d_lo <- (b_between - 1.96 * se_between) * ln_seq
  lp_d_hi <- (b_between + 1.96 * se_between) * ln_seq

  df_between <- tibble(
    gaming_min = ln_seq * 10,
    exc.prob  = pnorm((alpha_j_d - lp_d)    / denom_d, lower.tail = FALSE),
    asymp.LCL = pnorm((alpha_j_d - lp_d_lo) / denom_d, lower.tail = FALSE),
    asymp.UCL = pnorm((alpha_j_d - lp_d_hi) / denom_d, lower.tail = FALSE)
  )

  x_range_a  <- c(-60, 90)
  x_breaks_a <- seq(-60, 90, by = 30)

  between_stats <- list(
    mean   = mean(diary_ocat$late_night_between, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(diary_ocat$late_night_between, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75    = quantile(diary_ocat$late_night_between, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90    = quantile(diary_ocat$late_night_between, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  pA_dist <- ggplot(
    data.frame(x = diary_ocat$late_night_between[!is.na(diary_ocat$late_night_between)]),
    aes(x = x)
  ) +
    geom_density(fill = "gray70", color = "gray50", alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$median, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$mean,   linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p75,    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p90,    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks_a, labels = paste0(x_breaks_a, " min"), limits = x_range_a) +
    labs(y = "Density", x = NULL, title = "A") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x      = element_blank(),
      axis.title.x     = element_blank(),
      plot.margin      = margin(5, 5, 0, 5),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
    )

  # Shared y-axis limits — computed after Panel B, applied to both
  y_top_a <- max(df_between$asymp.UCL, na.rm = TRUE)
  y_ann_a <- y_top_a * 0.88

  pA_main <- ggplot(df_between, aes(x = gaming_min, y = exc.prob)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$median, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$mean,   linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p75,    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p90,    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$median, y = y_ann_a, label = "Median",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$mean,   y = y_ann_a, label = "Mean",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$p75,    y = y_ann_a, label = "75th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$p90,    y = y_ann_a, label = "90th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = asymp.LCL, ymax = asymp.UCL),
                alpha = 0.4, fill = "#f46d43", color = "#f46d43",
                linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, color = "#d62828") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks_a, labels = paste0(x_breaks_a, " min"), limits = x_range_a) +
    labs(
      x = "Average Daily Late-Night Gaming, Centered (min/day)",
      y = "Predicted Probability of Poor Sleep Quality"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(0, 5, 5, 5))

  # ── PANEL B: H2 Within-Person x Chronotype Interaction ─────────────────────

  # Within-person gaming grid (per-10-min units)
  w_seq <- seq(-6, 9, by = 0.1)

  # Chronotype levels: -1 SD, 0, +1 SD
  chrono_sd <- sd(diary_ocat_h2$chronotype_centered, na.rm = TRUE)
  chrono_vals <- c(morning = -chrono_sd, mean = 0, evening = chrono_sd)
  chrono_colors <- c(morning = "#2166ac", mean = "#4d4d4d", evening = "#b2182b")
  chrono_labels <- c(
    morning = paste0("Morning (-1 SD = ", sprintf("%.1f", -chrono_sd), ")"),
    mean    = "Mean chronotype",
    evening = paste0("Evening (+1 SD = ", sprintf("%.1f", chrono_sd), ")")
  )

  # Per-imputation delta-method computation, then pool via Rubin's rules
  if (!is.null(diary_h2_rubin)) {
    m <- length(diary_h2_rubin$fits)

    # Coefficient names for the 4x4 submatrix
    sub_terms <- c("ln_within_10", "chronotype_centered",
                   "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered", "ln_between_10:chronotype_centered")
    # We only need: ln_within_10, chronotype_centered, ln_within_10:chronotype_centered
    # (between component held at 0, so ln_between_10 and its interaction drop out)

    # Storage for per-imputation predictions
    prob_list <- list()   # each element: matrix [length(w_seq), 3 chrono levels]
    var_list  <- list()   # same shape

    for (i in seq_len(m)) {
      fit_i <- diary_h2_rubin$fits[[i]]
      alpha_i  <- fit_i$alpha["Fair|Poor"]
      sigma_i  <- sqrt(fit_i$ST$pid[1, 1])
      denom_i  <- sqrt(1 + sigma_i^2)

      b_w   <- coef(fit_i)["ln_within_10"]
      b_c   <- coef(fit_i)["chronotype_centered"]
      b_wc  <- coef(fit_i)["ln_within_10:chronotype_centered"]

      V_full <- as.matrix(vcov(fit_i))
      # Subset to the 3 terms we need
      need <- c("ln_within_10", "chronotype_centered", "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered")
      V3 <- V_full[need, need, drop = FALSE]

      prob_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(w_seq), ncol = 3)
      var_mat  <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(w_seq), ncol = 3)
      colnames(prob_mat) <- colnames(var_mat) <- names(chrono_vals)

      for (j in seq_along(chrono_vals)) {
        c_val <- chrono_vals[j]
        # Linear predictor: eta = b_w * x + b_c * c + b_wc * x * c
        eta <- b_w * w_seq + b_c * c_val + b_wc * w_seq * c_val
        z   <- (alpha_i - eta) / denom_i
        prob_mat[, j] <- pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)

        # Gradient of P = 1 - Phi(z) w.r.t. (b_w, b_c, b_wc)
        # dP/d_theta = phi(z) / denom * d_eta/d_theta
        phi_z <- dnorm(z)
        # d_eta/d(b_w) = x;  d_eta/d(b_c) = c;  d_eta/d(b_wc) = x*c
        for (k in seq_along(w_seq)) {
          grad <- (phi_z[k] / denom_i) * c(w_seq[k], c_val, w_seq[k] * c_val)
          var_mat[k, j] <- as.numeric(t(grad) %*% V3 %*% grad)
        }
      }

      prob_list[[i]] <- prob_mat
      var_list[[i]]  <- var_mat
    }

    # Rubin's rules pooling across imputations
    # Qbar = mean of prob across imputations
    # Ubar = mean of within-imputation variance
    # B    = variance of prob across imputations
    # T    = Ubar + (1 + 1/m) * B
    prob_array <- array(unlist(prob_list), dim = c(length(w_seq), 3, m))
    var_array  <- array(unlist(var_list),  dim = c(length(w_seq), 3, m))

    Qbar <- apply(prob_array, c(1, 2), mean)
    Ubar <- apply(var_array,  c(1, 2), mean)
    B    <- apply(prob_array, c(1, 2), var)
    Ttot <- Ubar + (1 + 1/m) * B

    # Build prediction data frame
    df_h2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(chrono_vals), function(j) {
      tibble(
        gaming_min = w_seq * 10,
        chrono     = names(chrono_vals)[j],
        exc.prob   = Qbar[, j],
        asymp.LCL  = pmax(Qbar[, j] - 1.96 * sqrt(Ttot[, j]), 0),
        asymp.UCL  = Qbar[, j] + 1.96 * sqrt(Ttot[, j])
      )
    }))
    df_h2$chrono <- factor(df_h2$chrono, levels = names(chrono_vals))
  } else {
    # Complete-case fallback (single model)
    fit_h2 <- readRDS("output/models/diary_model_h2_sleepquality.rds")
    alpha_h2  <- fit_h2$alpha["Fair|Poor"]
    sigma_h2  <- sqrt(fit_h2$ST$pid[1, 1])
    denom_h2  <- sqrt(1 + sigma_h2^2)

    b_w  <- coef(fit_h2)["ln_within_10"]
    b_c  <- coef(fit_h2)["chronotype_centered"]
    b_wc <- coef(fit_h2)["ln_within_10:chronotype_centered"]
    V_full <- as.matrix(vcov(fit_h2))
    need <- c("ln_within_10", "chronotype_centered", "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered")
    V3 <- V_full[need, need, drop = FALSE]

    df_h2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(chrono_vals), function(j) {
      c_val <- chrono_vals[j]
      eta <- b_w * w_seq + b_c * c_val + b_wc * w_seq * c_val
      z   <- (alpha_h2 - eta) / denom_h2
      prob <- pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)
      phi_z <- dnorm(z)
      se_vec <- vapply(seq_along(w_seq), function(k) {
        grad <- (phi_z[k] / denom_h2) * c(w_seq[k], c_val, w_seq[k] * c_val)
        sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% V3 %*% grad))
      }, numeric(1))
      tibble(
        gaming_min = w_seq * 10,
        chrono     = names(chrono_vals)[j],
        exc.prob   = prob,
        asymp.LCL  = pmax(prob - 1.96 * se_vec, 0),
        asymp.UCL  = prob + 1.96 * se_vec
      )
    }))
    df_h2$chrono <- factor(df_h2$chrono, levels = names(chrono_vals))
  }

  # Within-person predictor distribution stats
  x_range_b  <- c(-60, 90)
  x_breaks_b <- seq(-60, 90, by = 30)

  within_stats <- list(
    mean   = mean(diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75    = quantile(diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90    = quantile(diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  pB_dist <- ggplot(
    data.frame(x = diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within[!is.na(diary_ocat_h2$late_night_within)]),
    aes(x = x)
  ) +
    geom_density(fill = "gray70", color = "gray50", alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$median, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$mean,   linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$p75,    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$p90,    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks_b, labels = paste0(x_breaks_b, " min"), limits = x_range_b) +
    labs(y = NULL, x = NULL, title = "B") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x      = element_blank(),
      axis.title.x     = element_blank(),
      plot.margin      = margin(5, 5, 0, 5),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
    )

  # Shared y-axis limits across both panels
  y_top_b <- max(df_h2$asymp.UCL, na.rm = TRUE)
  y_top   <- max(y_top_a, y_top_b)
  y_lim   <- c(0, y_top * 1.2)

  # Re-compute annotation positions with shared y limits
  y_ann <- y_top * 0.88

  # Update Panel A main with shared limits
  pA_main <- pA_main +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = y_lim)

  # Re-set annotation y positions in Panel A
  pA_main <- ggplot(df_between, aes(x = gaming_min, y = exc.prob)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$median, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$mean,   linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p75,    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = between_stats$p90,    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$median, y = y_ann, label = "Median",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$mean,   y = y_ann, label = "Mean",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$p75,    y = y_ann, label = "75th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = between_stats$p90,    y = y_ann, label = "90th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = asymp.LCL, ymax = asymp.UCL),
                alpha = 0.4, fill = "#f46d43", color = "#f46d43",
                linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, color = "#d62828") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks_a, labels = paste0(x_breaks_a, " min"), limits = x_range_a) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = y_lim) +
    labs(
      x = "Average Daily Late-Night Gaming, Centered (min/day)",
      y = "Predicted Probability of Poor Sleep Quality"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(0, 5, 5, 5))

  # Panel B main plot
  pB_main <- ggplot(df_h2, aes(x = gaming_min, y = exc.prob, color = chrono, fill = chrono)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$median, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$mean,   linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$p75,    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = within_stats$p90,    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
    annotate("text", x = within_stats$median, y = y_ann, label = "Median",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = within_stats$mean,   y = y_ann, label = "Mean",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = within_stats$p75,    y = y_ann, label = "75th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = within_stats$p90,    y = y_ann, label = "90th %ile",
             angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, size = 3, color = "gray40") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = asymp.LCL, ymax = asymp.UCL),
                alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = chrono_colors, labels = chrono_labels, name = "Chronotype") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = chrono_colors, labels = chrono_labels, name = "Chronotype") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks_b, labels = paste0(x_breaks_b, " min"), limits = x_range_b) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = y_lim) +
    labs(
      x = "Daily Late-Night Gaming Deviation (min, within-person)",
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.margin      = margin(0, 5, 5, 5),
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      legend.direction = "horizontal"
    )

  # Combine: (density / main) for each panel, then side by side
  panelA <- (pA_dist / pA_main) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3))
  panelB <- (pB_dist / pB_main) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3))

  (panelA | panelB) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1))
} else {
  message("Diary H1/H2 models not found. Run with eval_diary_imputed = TRUE first.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diary-h1h2
#| tbl-cap: "Diary CLMM Regression Results: H1 (Direct Effects) and H2 (Chronotype Moderation) for Sleep Quality"
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# runtime: ~30-60s with params$icc_full = false (default; ICC from each
#          bundle's first fit only). With params$icc_full = true, ~15-18 min
#          on cold render (performance::icc() averaged over 60 imputations
#          × 2 bundles) and essentially free on subsequent renders thanks
#          to the disk-backed scalar cache in manuscript_cache/icc/. See
#          helpers.R get_custom_rows_pooled().
library(tinytable)
library(modelsummary)

# Use imputed (Rubin's rules) models when available, else fall back to complete-case
diary_use_imputed <- !is.null(diary_h1_rubin) && !is.null(diary_h2_rubin)

if (diary_use_imputed) {
  diary_models_combined <- list(
    "H1: Sleep Quality" = diary_h1_rubin$pooled,
    "H2: Chronotype Moderation" = diary_h2_rubin$pooled
  )
  # Coef names from pooled summary
  all_coef_names <- unique(c(
    summary(diary_h1_rubin$pooled)$term,
    summary(diary_h2_rubin$pooled)$term
  ))
  diary_add_rows <- get_custom_rows_pooled(
    list("H1: Sleep Quality" = diary_h1_rubin, "H2: Chronotype Moderation" = diary_h2_rubin),
    icc_method = if (isTRUE(params$icc_full)) "averaged" else "structural"
  )
  tbl_note_source <- "Estimates pooled across 60 multiply imputed datasets using Rubin's rules."
} else {
  diary_model_h1_loaded <- tryCatch(readRDS("output/models/diary_model_h1_sleepquality.rds"), error = function(e) NULL)
  diary_model_h2_loaded <- tryCatch(readRDS("output/models/diary_model_h2_sleepquality.rds"), error = function(e) NULL)
  diary_models_combined <- list(
    "H1: Sleep Quality" = diary_model_h1_loaded,
    "H2: Chronotype Moderation" = diary_model_h2_loaded
  )
  all_coef_names <- if (!is.null(diary_model_h1_loaded) && !is.null(diary_model_h2_loaded)) {
    unique(c(names(coef(diary_model_h1_loaded)), names(coef(diary_model_h2_loaded))))
  } else character(0)
  diary_add_rows <- get_custom_rows(Filter(Negate(is.null), diary_models_combined))
  tbl_note_source <- "Complete-case estimates (imputed diary models not found)."
}

diary_any_model <- !is.null(diary_models_combined[["H1: Sleep Quality"]]) &&
                   !is.null(diary_models_combined[["H2: Chronotype Moderation"]])

if (diary_any_model) {
  diary_coef_map <- c(
    "ln_within_10"                       = "LN gaming within-person (per 10 min)",
    "ln_between_10"                      = "LN gaming between-person (per 10 min)",
    "chronotype_centered"                = "Chronotype (h, centered)",
    "ln_within_10:chronotype_centered"   = "LN within × Chronotype",
    "chronotype_centered:ln_between_10"  = "LN between × Chronotype",
    "age_scaled"                         = "Age (scaled)",
    "bmi_scaled"                         = "BMI (scaled)",
    "SES_index_scaled"                   = "SES (scaled)"
  )

  weekend_map <- c()
  if ("is_weekendTRUE" %in% all_coef_names) {
    weekend_map <- c("is_weekendTRUE" = "Day: Weekend")
  } else if ("is_weekend" %in% all_coef_names) {
    weekend_map <- c("is_weekend" = "Day: Weekend")
  }
  diary_coef_map <- c(diary_coef_map, weekend_map)

  tt_diary <- modelsummary(
    diary_models_combined,
    fmt = fmt_sprintf("%.2f"),
    estimate = "{estimate}{stars}\n[{conf.low}, {conf.high}]",
    statistic = NULL,
    gof_omit = "AIC|BIC|Log|RMSE|R2|ICC|Num|nobs",
    coef_map = diary_coef_map,
    add_rows = diary_add_rows,
    notes = c(
      "+ p < 0.10, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001",
      "LN = late-night. Confidence intervals shown in brackets below each estimate.",
      tbl_note_source,
      "Cumulative link mixed models (random intercept for participant) on 5-level ordinal sleep quality (positive coefficients = higher probability of worse sleep). Both H1 and H2 use probit link. Late-night gaming expressed per 10 minutes; chronotype in centered hours; age, BMI, SES scaled within the diary subsample. Region excluded: all diary participants are US-only.",
      "Within = daily deviation from person mean; Between = person mean - grand mean."
    ),
    output = "tinytable"
  ) |>
    tinytable::format_tt(j = 2:3, linebreak = "\n")
  dir.create("output/tables", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  tryCatch(
    save_tt(tt_diary, "output/tables/tbl-diary-h1h2.png", overwrite = TRUE),
    error = function(e) message("Note: PNG export skipped (", e$message, ")")
  )
  tt_diary
} else {
  cat("Diary models not found. Render with `-P refit_diary_imputed:true` to generate them.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: discussion-equivalence-prep
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Response-scale ROPE thresholds used in the Discussion equivalence prose.
# Originally defined later in the Equivalence appendix, but Quarto/knitr
# evaluates inline R in source order, so these need to be available before
# the Discussion's inline refs (fmt0(eq_rope_sleep_h1b_min), etc.).
# Computed from the on-disk Rubin bundles so the values stay in sync.
.eq_sd_y <- function(path, response) {
  b <- readRDS(path); f <- b$fits[[1]]@frame
  sd(f[[response]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
.eq_sd_prod <- function(path, a, b_) {
  b <- readRDS(path); f <- b$fits[[1]]@frame
  sd(f[[a]] * f[[b_]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

eq_sd_sleep_h1b   <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h1b_rubin.rds", "total_hours_sleep")
eq_sd_wemwbs_h1d  <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h1d_rubin.rds", "wemwbs")
eq_sd_ess_h1c     <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h1c_rubin.rds", "epsTotal")

eq_rope_sleep_h1b_hr  <- 0.1 * eq_sd_sleep_h1b
eq_rope_sleep_h1b_min <- 60 * eq_rope_sleep_h1b_hr
eq_rope_wemwbs_h1d    <- 0.1 * eq_sd_wemwbs_h1d
eq_rope_ess_h1c       <- 0.1 * eq_sd_ess_h1c

eq_sd_sleep_h2b       <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h2b_rubin.rds", "total_hours_sleep")
eq_sd_wemwbs_h2d      <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h2d_rubin.rds", "wemwbs")
eq_sd_ess_h2c         <- .eq_sd_y("output/models/imputed_h2c_rubin.rds", "epsTotal")
eq_rope_sleep_h2b_min <- 60 * 0.1 * eq_sd_sleep_h2b
eq_rope_wemwbs_h2d    <- 0.1 * eq_sd_wemwbs_h2d
eq_rope_ess_h2c       <- 0.1 * eq_sd_ess_h2c

eq_rope_latent     <- 0.1
eq_rope_latent_pp  <- 100 * (pnorm(0.05) - pnorm(-0.05))

eq_sd_prod_h2      <- .eq_sd_prod("output/models/imputed_h2b_rubin.rds",
                                  "ln_monthly_avg_minutes_played_10",
                                  "msf_sc_centered")
```

# Discussion

This preregistered study examined whether late-night gaming is associated with poorer sleep quality, shorter sleep duration, greater daytime sleepiness, and lower wellbeing among adult gamers, and whether chronotype moderates these associations. Using objective telemetry linked to repeated self-report surveys, we found a consistent but small association between late-night gaming and sleep quality and little evidence that late-night gaming affects sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, or wellbeing directly. Under the same, pooled multiple-imputation analysis, chronotype did not meaningfully moderate any of the sleep- or wellbeing-related associations.

Of the four preregistered direct-effect hypotheses (H1a–H1d), only the association between late-night gaming and sleep quality was supported (H1a). Across the panel models (@tbl-h1-combined), each additional 10 minutes of average daily late-night gaming was associated with an approximate `r fmt_pp(h1a_marginal)` percentage-point increase in the marginal probability of reporting fairly bad or very bad sleep quality. This estimate was consistent across analytic specifications: the complete-case panel model (@tbl-appendix-h1-completecase) produced a closely matching `r fmt_pp(cc_h1a_marginal)` percentage-point increase; the exploratory diary between-person component (@tbl-diary-h1h2) (capturing stable individual differences in habitual late-night gaming) gave a comparable `r fmt_pp(diary_h1_marginal)` percentage-point increase in the probability of reporting poor or very poor daily sleep.

A sensitivity analysis substituting the continuous PSQI global score (@tbl-appendix-psqi-global) yielded directionally consistent positive fixed effects of late-night gaming on total PSQI points (imputed: `r psqi_global_imp_b_ci`; complete-case: `r psqi_global_cc_b_ci`), where the coefficient denotes the change in PSQI global score per additional 10 late-night minutes per day. Translated to the probability scale, these correspond to an approximate `r fmt_pp(psqi_global_imp_marginal)` (imputed) / `r fmt_pp(psqi_global_cc_marginal)` (complete-case) percentage-point increase in the probability of exceeding the PSQI poor-sleeper cutoff (> 5) at the sample mean. Linearity checks for the primary H1a specification, comparing natural-spline alternatives to the linear form on the gaming-exposure term, produced similar slopes at representative exposure levels (@tbl-appendix-panel-h1-spline-bic; @fig-appendix-panel-h1-spline-bic), supporting the preregistered linear parameterisation.

The convergence of these findings across different operationalisations of sleep quality, analytic strategies, and study designs strengthens our confidence that the association, though small, is genuine. Our observational design does not permit causal inference: although the association is robust across specifications, we cannot determine whether late-night gaming itself degrades sleep quality, whether poor sleepers are drawn to late-night gaming, or whether a third, uncontrolled factor drives both.

While remaining direct-effect hypotheses were not supported, these are not merely underpowered nulls: frequentist equivalence tests (TOST; @lakens2017equivalence) allow us to actively accept the null hypothesis of a negligible effect. For all three non-significant direct effects (H1b–H1d), the 90% confidence intervals fell entirely within the region of practical equivalence (±0.1 × SD(*y*); see @tbl-appendix-equivalence), providing positive evidence that any true effects of late-night gaming in this sample are too small to be of practical consequence. In substantive terms, we can rule out effects larger than roughly ±`r fmt0(eq_rope_sleep_h1b_min)` minutes of nightly sleep per one-SD increase in late-night gaming (H1b) — far below the amount that would plausibly affect next-day functioning; ±`r fmt1(eq_rope_ess_h1c)` points on the 0–24 Epworth Sleepiness Scale (H1c) — much smaller than the ~5-point gap separating normal from clinically excessive daytime sleepiness [@johns1991new]; and ±`r fmt1(eq_rope_wemwbs_h1d)` points on the SWEMWBS wellbeing scale (H1d), well under the ~1 to 3-point change regarded as clinically meaningful [@maheswaran2012evaluating]. In other words, even the largest effects compatible with our data would be undetectable against the everyday variability in sleep, mood, and alertness.

These findings speak to the sleep displacement hypothesis, which posits that late-night gaming displaces sleep time, thereby shortening sleep duration and producing daytime sleepiness [@twenge2019more; @lemola2011habitual; @exelmans2015sleep]. Reduced sleep duration, the core prediction of that account is directly contradicted by our equivalence-confirmed null for H1b, and the absence of any detectable effect on daytime sleepiness (H1c) removes a key downstream consequence that would be expected if meaningful displacement were occurring. Taken together, the pattern of results argues against a displacement explanation: sleep duration and alertness were preserved, while subjective sleep quality alone was modestly worse. The residual quality effect is multiply realisable: at least three non-displacement mechanisms predict the same "quality down, duration preserved" signature. Pre-sleep physiological arousal or cognitive stimulation from gaming [@king2013impact] is one; an attribution mechanism whereby players who game late at night perceive their sleep as poorer regardless of whether its duration or architecture is objectively altered is a second; and compensatory phase delay, in which gamers delay rather than shorten their sleep window so that duration and alertness are preserved but the sleep occurs at a circadian phase misaligned with their work-week schedule — leaving subjective quality degraded even when the hours are intact, is a third. The classical arousal account is not unambiguously preferred among these: it typically predicts disrupted sleep architecture — slow-wave and REM suppression and lengthened sleep-onset latency — with downstream daytime costs such as poorer next-day memory and alertness [@dworak2007impact; @higuchi2005effects; @weaver2010effect], and our equivalence-confirmed null on daytime sleepiness (H1c) does not see that cost. The data therefore rule against displacement and are compatible with, but do not positively single out, any one of the surviving candidates; self-report instruments alone cannot adjudicate among them. This quality-without-duration dissociation is mirrored in contemporary adult evidence. A nationally representative US survey found that pre-bedtime device use was associated with poorer self-reported sleep quality and greater sleep deficits but showed no association with sleep duration after adjustment for sociodemographic covariates [@carlson2026technology]; another adult sample contrasting habitual gamers (≥7 h/week) with occasional and non-gamers found no group differences in PSQI global score, sleep duration, or daytime sleepiness, and weekly hours of play actually predicted lower daytime sleepiness and dysfunction in the continuous analyses [@derosa2023habitual]. Yet another adult cohort sits at the edge of this pattern, reporting elevated odds of excessive daytime sleepiness for adults who often play games before bed [@schrempft2024bedtime]; the divergence may reflect design choices (dichotomised Epworth cutoff, categorical Likert exposure rather than a continuous one) that concentrate signal in heavy users in a way our continuous, population-mean equivalence test explicitly bounds.

The null finding for wellbeing (H1d) sits within a growing body of trace-data evidence that objectively logged gameplay is at most weakly related to mental wellbeing. A narrative review of 13 proposed mechanisms argues that gaming operates through offsetting pathways that may involve relaxation, need satisfaction, and social connection on one side; displacement of sleep, exercise, and social activity, plus pre-sleep arousal on the other, making a small or null net association with global wellbeing the expected result [@ballou2024mechanisms]. The empirical record agrees: large telemetry studies consistently find trivial playtime–wellbeing links [@johannes2021video; @vuorre2022time; @ballou2025perceived], with perceived value of play and not hours logged driving wellbeing outcomes. Our null fits this pattern: the hedonic benefits of late-night gaming appear to offset any modest cost routed through perceived sleep quality.

## Chronotype Moderation

The preregistered moderation hypotheses (H2) predicted that evening chronotype would amplify the negative associations between late-night gaming and all four outcomes. These predictions were grounded in theories of circadian misalignment and social jetlag, which hold that evening chronotypes are especially affected by late-night stimulation because it exacerbates the existing misalignment between their endogenous sleep–wake rhythm and socially imposed schedules [@zhong2025electronic; @kortesoja2023latenight]. None of the preregistered moderation hypotheses were supported under the pooled multiple-imputation analysis: the chronotype × late-night gaming interaction was non-significant for sleep quality (H2a: `r h2a_ln_minutes_msf`), sleep duration (H2b: `r h2b_ln_minutes_msf`), daytime sleepiness (H2c: `r h2c_ln_minutes_msf`), and wellbeing (H2d: `r h2d_ln_minutes_msf`).

Frequentist equivalence tests with a ROPE rescaled to the coefficient's native units (±0.1 × SD(*y*) / SD(*x*); see @tbl-appendix-equivalence) supported practical equivalence for the H2b, H2c, and H2d interactions. The H2a interaction was undecided: the 90% CI was narrow but extended marginally beyond the lower bound of the latent-scale ROPE.

The exploratory diary data told a similar story at the trait level: the between-person chronotype × late-night gaming interaction was small and non-significant (`r diary_h2_between_chrono`), indicating that the habitual association between late-night gaming and nightly sleep quality did not meaningfully vary across chronotypes. The within-person interaction did reach conventional significance (`r diary_h2_within_chrono`), suggesting that on days when evening-type participants gamed more than usual, the day-to-day link to sleep quality was paradoxically somewhat weaker rather than stronger; a finding that runs against the preregistered prediction and that we treat as exploratory. Notably, the diary model did show a significant main effect of chronotype on nightly sleep quality (`r diary_h2_chrono_main`), with later chronotypes reporting worse sleep on average. A pattern of trait-level chronotype penalty for sleep quality, but no amplification of the late-night-gaming effect by chronotype is consistent with the broader circadian-misalignment literature without supporting the more specific claim that evening types are differentially harmed by late-night play.

The largely null moderation results have several possible explanations. Evening-type gamers may have developed coping mechanisms or adapted sleep routines that buffer them against the effects of late-night play, for instance, by habitually sleeping in later or napping to compensate. More likely, the circadian misalignment pathway may simply be weaker than previously assumed in adult populations who have more autonomy over their schedules than the adolescent samples on which much of the chronotype–technology literature is based [@bruni2015technology; @reardon2023adolescent]. Consensus on how to operationalise problematic gaming in adults with greater scheduling autonomy is also still being established [@costa2019current; @mannikko2020problematic], which complicates direct read-across from adolescent-focused effect estimates. This reading is corroborated by independent adult-cohort evidence: @schrempft2024bedtime explicitly tested chronotype as both a mediator and a moderator of the bedtime-media-sleep link in 4,188 adults, and found that evening chronotypes engaged in pre-sleep media more frequently but were not differentially harmed by it, exactly the pattern our pre-registered H2 equivalence tests recover.

## Contextualising the effect

Viewed at the per-person, per-night scale, the association is small in absolute terms. At the marginal rate of `r fmt_pp(h1a_marginal)` percentage points per 10 minutes, even a gamer averaging an hour of play past 11pm would see only a roughly `r fmt_pp(h1a_marginal, minutes = 60, digits = 0)` percentage-point increase in the probability of reporting poor sleep quality. Against the backdrop of `r sprintf("%.0f%%", poor_pct_ana)` of participants already qualifying as poor sleepers by PSQI criteria, late-night gaming appears to be a minor per-person contributor to an issue with broader origins that likely involves work schedules, general screen use, caffeine consumption, and other lifestyle factors not captured here.

It is useful to anchor the implied per-hour magnitude against other modifiable lifestyle influences on adult sleep. At roughly `r fmt_pp(h1a_marginal, minutes = 60, digits = 0)` percentage points per hour, the sleep-quality cost of late-night gaming appears to be in the same broad range as the perceived sleep-quality cost reported for a high (400 mg) dose of caffeine consumed within four hours of bedtime [@gardiner2025dose]. This comparison is most directly interpretable for our exploratory diary substudy, which used a structurally similar single-item nightly sleep-quality rating; there, the between-person estimate (`r fmt_pp(diary_h1_marginal)` percentage points per 10 min of habitual late-night gaming) aligned closely with the panel PSQI result. A comparable benchmark on the continuous PSQI scale comes from @yan2024chronobiological, who report a ≈0.39-point higher PSQI total score for adults in the latest vs earliest tertile of last-meal time (a ≈3-hour shift). For a contrast of similar practical magnitude in our data — moving from ~`r psqi_contrast_low_min` min/day to ~`r sprintf("%g", psqi_contrast_high_min/60)` h/day of late-night gaming — the panel PSQI sensitivity model implies a ≈`r sprintf("%.2f", psqi_global_imp_contrast)`-point increase, of comparable order but somewhat smaller, suggesting that the per-person sleep-quality penalty of habitual late-night gaming sits below that of habitually late evening meal timing.

That we found this effect specifically for sleep quality — rather than duration, sleepiness, or wellbeing — narrows the field to mechanisms that disturb perceived sleep without producing a detectable downstream cost, namely the three candidates flagged above (pre-sleep arousal, attribution, and compensatory phase delay). The exploratory diary decomposition further constrains which of these is most plausible. The H1a-analog signal is carried almost entirely by the between-person component (`r diary_h1_between`), with the within-person, same-night estimate non-significant (`r diary_h1_within`): habitually late-night-gaming participants reported worse sleep on average, but nights on which a given participant gamed more than their own average were not reliably followed by worse sleep that night. An acute pre-sleep arousal mechanism predicts precisely the latter within-person, same-night degradation, so the diary pattern sits more comfortably with trait-level processes such as a durable attributional style, stable lifestyle confounding, or selection of more arousable players into habitual late-night play than with acute arousal per se. Because our sleep measures are all self-reported, we cannot distinguish an attributional process from a genuine change in sleep architecture; wearable-based ambulatory measurement would be needed to adjudicate.

A small per-night effect can nonetheless carry weight when it is sustained over time and aggregated across a common behaviour. Restricting sleep by only about an hour can still disturb emotion regulation [@tomaso2021effect] and undermine cognitive and behavioural performance [@belenky2003patterns]; if that restriction is maintained for two weeks, losses in alertness and working memory can rival those seen after an entire night without sleep [@vandongen2003cumulative]. Repeated small shifts in nightly sleep quality from habitual late-night play may therefore matter for mood, vigilance, and cognition over weeks and months, even if any single night looks unremarkable. Benchmarks tailored to sleep outcomes support this interpretation: Panjeh and colleagues' recalibration from 72 effect sizes in 65 sleep-quality intervention trials [@panjeh2023establishing] maps "small", "medium", and "large" to Cohen's *d* of roughly 0.18, 0.33, and 0.56 — below the usual 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 anchors. Judged against those sleep-specific standards, the cumulative impact of 1–2 hours of late-night gaming falls in the small-to-medium band, whereas the same pattern might look small on the generic Cohen scale.

Population burden adds another layer. De Rosa and colleagues [-@derosa2024videogaming] note that video gaming is now one of the most widespread adult leisure exposures and that sleep outcomes track how intensively and how often people play, so a shallow per-night gradient can still shift the upper tail of poor sleep when layered onto a common behaviour. Public-health importance depends on both per-person effect magnitude and how prevalent the behaviour is and on this combined view, our findings sit alongside a broader literature reporting statistically detectable but per-person modest associations between digital media use and psychological outcomes.

A key gap in the existing literature is the near-complete absence of timing-specific measurement: @kristensen2021problematic noted that none of the studies in their systematic review registered the time of day gaming took place. Most adult gaming-and-sleep studies consequently operationalise exposure as aggregate daily volume or as binary/categorical problematic-gaming contrasts, which are likely to dilute any signal concentrated in the pre-sleep window. A parallel gap arises at the device-specific level: even a recent nationally representative US adult survey [@carlson2026technology] collapsed pre-bedtime TV and gaming-console use into a single category, an acknowledged limitation given that passively watching TV and actively playing video games imply very different levels of interactivity and likely have differential impacts on sleep. Our telemetry-based, continuous, time-of-day-specific operationalisation of late-night play is deliberately designed to isolate exactly that window, and the fact that we find a small but robust association only for sleep quality is consistent with reviews identifying pre-sleep timing, arousal, and session duration as key moderators of gaming's effect on sleep [@derosa2024videogaming; @kemp2021sleep]. That the effect is detectable at all under a stringent, preregistered, multiply-imputed longitudinal specification suggests that timing-specific exposures capture signal that aggregate-volume measures may miss.

## Limitations

Constraints bound the scope of our findings. First, our telemetry captures console and PC play but excludes mobile platforms, which account for a substantial share of late-night leisure — particularly in-bed use that bypasses "household curfews" and serves as a pre-sleep emotional-regulation tool. Late-night minutes that shifted to phones therefore go unmeasured, likely attenuating observed associations, and we cannot separate gaming-specific effects from the broader bundle of nocturnal screen behaviours (short-form video, messaging, doomscrolling) that share the same devices.

Second, even within the platforms we do observe, session-level logs cannot distinguish active engagement from idle time, an ambiguity that is especially acute at night when consoles may stay on while players drift off or step away. This can inflate exposure and produce spurious late-night "activity" that does not reflect cognitive arousal. Relatedly, session logs do not record game content or in-session intensity, so arousal-inducing genres (competitive, horror, fast-paced action) cannot be separated from more routine play — a moderator that adult-focused reviews identify as plausibly shaping sleep effects [@derosa2024videogaming; @kemp2021sleep].

Third, the analytic sample is restricted to adults recruited from UK- and US-based Prolific panels. Younger players have different sleep physiology, school schedules, parental oversight, and motivational profiles, and our estimates should not be extrapolated to pediatric or older populations. Prolific panels themselves are self-selected online workers with reliable broadband, high digital literacy, and tolerance for repeated surveys; eligibility filters around residency, language, and compliance further exclude players in other linguistic and regulatory contexts, as well as shift workers, caregivers, lower-income players, and those engaged in more extreme or stigmatized gaming profiles. Taken together, these constraints mean our findings speak most directly to digitally engaged young adults in the UK and US who play on major console and PC ecosystems; extension to other regions, life stages, device ecologies should await complementary data sources.

## Future Directions

Future work would benefit from combining telemetry with finer-grained metadata on game content, arousal level, and session proximity to bedtime, and from extending logging to mobile platforms so that the full pre-sleep screen bundle can be measured rather than inferred. Linking telemetry to ambulatory physiological measurements (e.g., consumer-grade actigraphy, heart-rate variability, or ambient light sensing) would additionally allow researchers to separate subjective perception of sleep disturbance from objective architecture, which our self-report instruments could not disentangle, and would be the natural way to adjudicate among the three non-displacement candidates the present design leaves on the table — acute pre-sleep arousal (which predicts within-person, same-night HRV elevation, lengthened sleep-onset latency, and reduced slow-wave activity), attribution (which predicts no such physiological signature), and compensatory phase delay (which predicts a within-person delay in actigraphic sleep onset and offset without a duration loss). Such measurements would also index mechanistic pathways our session-level logs cannot — notably evening light exposure, which has been proposed as a contributor to gaming-related sleep disturbance alongside physiological arousal [@hartmann2019effects]. The rapid growth of consumer wearables (smartwatches, fitness trackers, and rings) now reach a substantial share of the populations from which gaming cohorts are recruited makes participant-initiated data donation an increasingly tractable route to such measurements. Rather than provisioning research-grade devices to every participant, future telemetry studies could invite players to donate sleep and activity records from devices they already wear, mirroring the platform-level donation model used here for play behaviour. This would lower per-participant cost, extend follow-up windows beyond what dedicated instrumentation typically allows, and bring objective sleep estimates into the same within-person, high-frequency frame as the telemetry itself, while raising its own questions about device heterogeneity, missingness, and the selection pressures introduced by wearable ownership.

Second, the observational design of this study limits the strength of causal claims that can be drawn from any single estimate. One natural next step is to embed telemetry-based exposures within a target trial emulation framework [@hernan2016using; @hernan2022target], which makes the hypothetical randomized experiment explicit (e.g., a late-night play session versus none on a given weekday). Target trial emulation is particularly well suited to device-use research because the relevant question is rarely "do gamers sleep worse than non-gamers" but rather "does the same person sleep worse on nights they play late than on nights they do not." High-frequency telemetry naturally supports such within-person contrasts, and pairing it with g-methods or sequential exchangeability assumptions would allow future work to move from associational gradients toward more interpretable, policy-relevant causal estimates while keeping each individual as their own control.

The telemetry–survey linkage protocol piloted in Open Play is, in principle, portable: with appropriate ethical safeguards, assent procedures, and clinical validation, an analogous continuous-telemetry approach could be used to study adolescents and problematic gamers, populations in which the timing-specific effects of late-night play are most hotly contested and where aggregate self-report measures are especially vulnerable to recall bias. Extending the present methodology to those populations rather than extrapolating our estimates to them is, in our view, the most productive next step.

## Panel: Wave-Level Missingness

We summarised the extent of missingness for the key self-report outcomes across each survey wave in the raw data before imputation. The `Observations` column reports the number of participants in a wave who completed at least one of the listed measures; the percentages in each row are calculated relative to that wave-specific participant count.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix-wave-missingness
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Wave-level missingness for key self-report measures (pre-imputation data)"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tinytable)

# Counts/Observations precomputed in the `wave-missingness-compute` chunk
# (above # Methods) so the Methods prose and this appendix table share one
# source of truth for the per-wave missingness numbers.
wave_missing_table <- wave_missing_counts |>
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(wave_missing_flags),
      ~if_else(
        Observations > 0,
        sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", .x, 100 * .x / Observations),
        sprintf("%d (--)", .x)
      )
    )
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Sleep quality (PSQI item 6)` = psqi_comp1_quality_imputed_flag,
    `Sleep duration (hours)` = total_hours_sleep_imputed_flag,
    `Daytime sleepiness (ESS)` = epsTotal_imputed_flag,
    `Wellbeing (SWEMWBS)` = wemwbs_imputed_flag
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(`Sleep quality (PSQI item 6)`, `Sleep duration (hours)`, `Daytime sleepiness (ESS)`),
      ~if_else(Wave %in% c(1L, 3L, 5L), "", .x)
    )
  )

tinytable::tt(
  wave_missing_table,
  caption = "Wave-level missingness for key self-report measures (pre-imputation data). Entries show the number and percentage of participants missing each measure within a wave."
)
```

## Panel: PSQI Global Score Sensitivity Analysis

This section presents a sensitivity analysis using the PSQI global score as an alternative sleep quality outcome. The PSQI global score is the sum of all 7 PSQI component scores (range 0-21, higher = worse sleep quality), providing a continuous measure compared to the ordinal PSQI item 6 outcome used in the pre-registered H1a hypothesis.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix-psqi-global
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity Analysis: PSQI Global Score Models (Imputed vs. Original)"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# PSQI-global Rubin bundles and complete-case fits are produced in the
# fit-psqi-global chunk earlier in the document (so the Discussion can
# reference their marginal pp/10-min effects). Here we just expose the
# pooled mipo objects that the table-building code below expects.
model_psqi_global_imputed        <- panel_psqi_rubin_base$pooled
model_psqi_global_imputed_chrono <- panel_psqi_rubin_chrono$pooled

# Create comparison table
# Match the row structure of the H1/H2 summaries for easier cross-referencing
psqi_label_lookup <- c(
  "ln_monthly_avg_minutes_played_10" = "Daily LN gaming (per 10 min/day, monthly)",
  "age_scaled" = "Age (scaled)",
  "bmi_scaled" = "BMI (scaled)",
  "SES_index_scaled" = "SES (scaled)",
  "msf_sc_centered" = "Chronotype (h, centered)",
  "ln_monthly_avg_minutes_played_10:msf_sc_centered" = "LN gaming × Chronotype (h, monthly)",
  "isWeekend" = "Day: Weekend",
  "SD (Intercept pid)" = "SD (Intercept | Participant)",
  "SD (Intercept gender)" = "SD (Intercept | Gender)",
  "SD (Observations)" = "SD (Residual)"
)

psqi_base_terms <- c(
  "ln_monthly_avg_minutes_played_10",
  "age_scaled",
  "bmi_scaled",
  "SES_index_scaled"
)

psqi_moderator_terms <- c(
  "msf_sc_centered",
  "ln_monthly_avg_minutes_played_10:msf_sc_centered"
)

psqi_random_terms <- c(
  "SD (Intercept pid)",
  "SD (Intercept gender)",
  "SD (Observations)"
)

psqi_base_map <- psqi_label_lookup[psqi_base_terms]
psqi_base_map <- psqi_base_map[!is.na(psqi_base_map)]

psqi_moderator_map <- psqi_label_lookup[psqi_moderator_terms]
psqi_moderator_map <- psqi_moderator_map[!is.na(psqi_moderator_map)]

psqi_random_map <- psqi_label_lookup[psqi_random_terms]
psqi_random_map <- psqi_random_map[!is.na(psqi_random_map)]

# Extract fixed effect names from all models (pooled mipo or lmerMod)
.get_term_names <- function(m) {
 if (inherits(m, "mipo")) {
    summary(m)$term
  } else {
    names(lme4::fixef(m))
  }
}
fixef_names <- unique(c(
  .get_term_names(model_psqi_global_imputed),
  .get_term_names(model_psqi_global_completecase),
  .get_term_names(model_psqi_global_imputed_chrono),
  .get_term_names(model_psqi_global_completecase_chrono)
))
fixef_names <- fixef_names[fixef_names != "(Intercept)"]

region_terms <- fixef_names[str_detect(fixef_names, "^region")]
region_map <- setNames(
  paste0("Region: ", str_replace_all(str_remove(region_terms, "^region"), "_", " ")),
  region_terms
)

weekend_term <- NULL
if ("isWeekend" %in% fixef_names) {
  weekend_term <- setNames(psqi_label_lookup["isWeekend"], "isWeekend")
} else if ("isWeekendTRUE" %in% fixef_names) {
  weekend_term <- setNames(psqi_label_lookup["isWeekend"], "isWeekendTRUE")
}

coef_map_psqi_global <- c(
  psqi_base_map,
  psqi_moderator_map,
  region_map,
  weekend_term,
  psqi_random_map
)
coef_map_psqi_global <- coef_map_psqi_global[!is.na(coef_map_psqi_global)]

psqi_models_list <- list(
  "Playtime (Imputed)" = model_psqi_global_imputed,
  "Chronotype × Playtime (Imputed)" = model_psqi_global_imputed_chrono,
  "Playtime (Complete-Case)" = model_psqi_global_completecase,
  "Chronotype × Playtime (Complete-Case)" = model_psqi_global_completecase_chrono
)

# Build custom rows: use Rubin bundles for imputed, single fits for complete-case
psqi_custom_rows <- {
  pooled_bundles <- list(
    "Playtime (Imputed)" = panel_psqi_rubin_base,
    "Chronotype × Playtime (Imputed)" = panel_psqi_rubin_chrono
  )
  cc_models <- list(
    "Playtime (Complete-Case)" = model_psqi_global_completecase,
    "Chronotype × Playtime (Complete-Case)" = model_psqi_global_completecase_chrono
  )
  pooled_rows <- get_custom_rows_pooled(
    pooled_bundles,
    icc_method = if (isTRUE(params$icc_full)) "averaged" else "structural"
  )
  cc_rows <- get_custom_rows(cc_models)
  # Merge: participant_df row then icc_df row
  merged <- pooled_rows
  for (col in names(cc_rows)) {
    if (col != "term") merged[[col]] <- cc_rows[[col]]
  }
  merged
}

psqi_group_cols <- seq_along(psqi_models_list) + 1

tt_psqi <- modelsummary(
  psqi_models_list,
  fmt = fmt_sprintf("%.2f"),
  estimate  = "{estimate} [{conf.low}, {conf.high}]{stars}",
  statistic = NULL,
  gof_omit = "AIC|BIC|Log|RMSE|R2|ICC|Num|nobs",
  coef_map = coef_map_psqi_global,
  add_rows = psqi_custom_rows,
  notes = c(
    "+ p < 0.10, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001",
    "PSQI global score range: 0-21 (higher = worse sleep quality)",
    "Confidence intervals shown in brackets.",
    "ICC = Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (adjusted)."
  ),
  output = "tinytable"
) |>
  group_tt(
    j = list("PSQI Global" = psqi_group_cols),
    part = "header"
  )
dir.create("output/tables", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
tryCatch(
  save_tt(tt_psqi, "output/tables/tbl-appendix-psqi-global.png", overwrite = TRUE),
  error = function(e) message("Note: PNG export skipped (", e$message, ")")
)
tt_psqi
```

## Diary: Daily Diary Subsample

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diary-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Daily Diary Subsample Characteristics"
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tinytable)

# Define diary samples
diary_total_pids <- unique(diary_long$pid)
diary_analytical_pids <- unique(diary_ocat$pid)

# Person-level summaries for diary sample
diary_person_total <- diary_long |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(
    n_diary_entries = n(),
    ln_gaming_min_day = mean(late_night_gaming_hours_24h * 60, na.rm = TRUE),
    any_ln_gaming_pct = 100 * mean(late_night_gaming_hours_24h > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(

                            chronotype_hours, chronotype_centered, no_alarm_free),

  )

diary_person_analytical <- diary_ocat |>
  group_by(pid) |>
  summarise(
    n_diary_entries = n(),
    ln_gaming_min_day = mean(late_night_minutes_trim, na.rm = TRUE),
    any_ln_gaming_pct = 100 * mean(late_night_minutes_trim > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    diary_ocat |> distinct(pid, age_scaled, bmi_scaled, SES_index_scaled, gender, region,
                            chronotype_hours, chronotype_centered, no_alarm_free),
    by = "pid"
  )

# Temporarily assign to master_data_total / master_data for helper functions
master_data_total_saved <- if (exists("master_data_total")) master_data_total else NULL
master_data_saved <- if (exists("master_data")) master_data else NULL
master_data_total <- diary_person_total
master_data <- diary_person_analytical

diary_summary_rows <- tibble(Characteristic = character(), Total = character(), Analytical = character())

# === A. Sociodemographics ===
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "**A. Sociodemographics**", Total = "", Analytical = ""))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "N participants",
         Total = as.character(length(diary_total_pids)),
         Analytical = as.character(length(diary_analytical_pids))))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "N diary entries",
         Total = as.character(nrow(diary_long)),
         Analytical = as.character(nrow(diary_ocat))))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "    Diary entries per person (Mdn, IQR)",
         Total = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f)",
           median(diary_person_total$n_diary_entries),
           IQR(diary_person_total$n_diary_entries)),
         Analytical = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f)",
           median(diary_person_analytical$n_diary_entries),
           IQR(diary_person_analytical$n_diary_entries))))

# Use intake data for age (unscaled)
diary_intake_total <- data.intake |> filter(pid %in% diary_total_pids)
diary_intake_analytical <- data.intake |> filter(pid %in% diary_analytical_pids)

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "Age",
         Total = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)",
           mean(as.numeric(diary_intake_total$age), na.rm = TRUE),
           sd(as.numeric(diary_intake_total$age), na.rm = TRUE)),
         Analytical = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)",
           mean(as.numeric(diary_intake_analytical$age), na.rm = TRUE),
           sd(as.numeric(diary_intake_analytical$age), na.rm = TRUE))))

# Gender
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "Gender", Total = "", Analytical = ""))

diary_gender_counts_total <- diary_person_total |>
  count(gender, name = "n_tot") |> filter(!is.na(gender))
diary_gender_counts_ana <- diary_person_analytical |>
  count(gender, name = "n_ana") |> filter(!is.na(gender))
diary_gender_merged <- diary_gender_counts_total |>
  full_join(diary_gender_counts_ana, by = "gender") |>
  mutate(n_tot = replace_na(n_tot, 0), n_ana = replace_na(n_ana, 0))

for (g in diary_gender_merged$gender) {
  row <- diary_gender_merged |> filter(gender == g)
  diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
    tibble(Characteristic = paste0("    ", g),
           Total = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", row$n_tot, 100 * row$n_tot / nrow(diary_person_total)),
           Analytical = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", row$n_ana, 100 * row$n_ana / nrow(diary_person_analytical))))
}

# BMI and SES
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  add_continuous("bmi_scaled", "BMI (scaled)", 2))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  add_continuous("SES_index_scaled", "SES (scaled)", 2))

# === B. Chronotype ===
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "**B. Chronotype**", Total = "", Analytical = ""))

no_alarm_n_tot <- sum(master_data_total$no_alarm_free, na.rm = TRUE)
no_alarm_pct_tot <- 100 * no_alarm_n_tot / sum(!is.na(master_data_total$no_alarm_free))
no_alarm_n_ana <- sum(master_data$no_alarm_free, na.rm = TRUE)
no_alarm_pct_ana <- 100 * no_alarm_n_ana / sum(!is.na(master_data$no_alarm_free))
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "No alarm on free days",
         Total = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", no_alarm_n_tot, no_alarm_pct_tot),
         Analytical = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", no_alarm_n_ana, no_alarm_pct_ana)))

msf_med_tot <- median(master_data_total$chronotype_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
msf_iqr_tot <- IQR(master_data_total$chronotype_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
msf_med_ana <- median(master_data$chronotype_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
msf_iqr_ana <- IQR(master_data$chronotype_hours, na.rm = TRUE)
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "    MSF~sc~ (HH:MM)",
         Total = sprintf("%s (%s)", hours_to_hhmm(msf_med_tot), hours_to_hhmm(msf_iqr_tot)),
         Analytical = sprintf("%s (%s)", hours_to_hhmm(msf_med_ana), hours_to_hhmm(msf_iqr_ana))))

# === C. Gaming ===
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "**C. Gaming**", Total = "", Analytical = ""))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  add_median_iqr("ln_gaming_min_day", "LN gaming (min/day, Mdn, IQR)", 1))

diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  add_continuous("any_ln_gaming_pct", "% entries with any LN gaming", 1))

# === D. Outcomes ===
diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
  tibble(Characteristic = "**D. Sleep Quality Distribution**", Total = "", Analytical = ""))

# Sleep quality distribution from diary entries (not person-level)
sq_dist_total <- diary_long |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_quality)) |>
  count(sleep_quality, name = "n_tot")
sq_dist_ana <- diary_ocat |>
  mutate(sleep_quality = as.character(sleep_quality_ord)) |>
  count(sleep_quality, name = "n_ana")
sq_dist <- sq_dist_total |>
  full_join(sq_dist_ana, by = "sleep_quality") |>
  mutate(n_tot = replace_na(n_tot, 0), n_ana = replace_na(n_ana, 0))
sq_n_total <- sum(sq_dist$n_tot)
sq_n_ana <- sum(sq_dist$n_ana)
sq_order <- c("Very poor", "Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Very good")
sq_dist <- sq_dist |> arrange(match(sleep_quality, sq_order))

for (sq in sq_dist$sleep_quality) {
  row <- sq_dist |> filter(sleep_quality == sq)
  diary_summary_rows <- bind_rows(diary_summary_rows,
    tibble(Characteristic = paste0("    ", sq),
           Total = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", row$n_tot, 100 * row$n_tot / sq_n_total),
           Analytical = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", row$n_ana, 100 * row$n_ana / sq_n_ana)))
}

# Restore master_data_total / master_data
if (!is.null(master_data_total_saved)) master_data_total <- master_data_total_saved
if (!is.null(master_data_saved)) master_data <- master_data_saved

# Display table
diary_header_rows <- which(str_detect(diary_summary_rows$Characteristic, "^\\*\\*"))
diary_sub_item_rows <- which(str_detect(diary_summary_rows$Characteristic, "^    ") &
                             !str_detect(diary_summary_rows$Characteristic, "^        "))

diary_tbl <- diary_summary_rows |>
  tt(
    caption = "Daily Diary Subsample Characteristics",
    notes = "Values are M (SD) unless noted. LN = late-night. Sleep quality distribution counts are at the diary-entry level."
  ) |>
  format_tt(j = 1, markdown = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 1, align = "l") |>
  style_tt(j = 2:3, align = "r") |>
  style_tt(i = diary_header_rows, bold = TRUE) |>
  format_tt(i = diary_header_rows, j = 1, fn = function(x) str_remove_all(x, "\\*\\*"))

if (length(diary_sub_item_rows) > 0) {
  diary_tbl <- diary_tbl |>
    style_tt(i = diary_sub_item_rows, j = 1, indent = 1) |>
    format_tt(i = diary_sub_item_rows, j = 1, fn = function(x) str_trim(x))
}
```
